name: Mere Exposure Effect
description: Repeated exposure to a stimulus can increase liking or preference even without reward or deeper evaluation. Familiarity itself can make a design, message, or brand element feel better.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to repeated brand cues, familiar navigation patterns, onboarding repetition, and UI elements that become easier to accept simply through exposure — with diminishing returns if overdone.
prevalence_note: Widely cited in branding, marketing-influenced UX, and familiarity-based design guidance, but the exact named effect is less central in mainstream UX teaching than the foundational-tier laws and biases.

findings.description: Across 208 studies conducted in the two decades following Zajonc's original monograph, the exposure-liking effect held robustly overall (r = 0.26) — one of the more consistently replicated findings in this corpus, in contrast to several other popular design-practice claims.
findings.source_title: Exposure and Affect: Overview and Meta-Analysis of Research, 1968-1987

findings.description: Mere repeated exposure to a stimulus — with no reinforcement, reward, or conscious evaluation required — is sufficient to increase a person's subsequent liking/preference for it, demonstrated across varied stimulus types (shapes, faces, nonsense words, unfamiliar characters).
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Monograph Supplement)

applications.title: A donor's photo on an e-card doubled charitable-giving participation at HMRC
applications.description: The UK's Behavioural Insights Team ran a field experiment with employees at HMRC (Her Majesty's Revenue and Customs), sending e-cards from a current charity donor asking colleagues to give. The control group's e-card had no photo of the donor; the treatment group's e-card included one. The control group's donation participation rate was 2.9%, compared to 6.4% in the treatment group -- including a photo of a familiar face more than doubled participation.
applications.ethical_note: Encouraging colleagues to donate to a legitimate charity using a genuine photo of a real donor is a straightforward, disclosed appeal with no deception involved -- there is no manipulative framing here, just a real behavioral lever (familiarity/exposure) applied to a prosocial ask.
